description:
A fortress has stood on the site of Château de Pray since the 6th century. The current 13th-century structure, later remodeled during the Renaissance, takes its name from Geoffroy de Pray. The château was long tied to families connected to the French royal court at nearby Château d'Amboise.

It became one of the first Loire châteaux to open as a hotel, in 1955. Today its 19 rooms are spread across the main château and its outbuildings, set in 5 hectares of wooded parkland with formal gardens, terraces, a vegetable garden and a heated pool. Interiors mix four-poster beds, antique furniture and period stained glass.

The château's 6th-century origins as a fortress site, well before the surviving 13th-century structure was built, point to a long continuity of habitation and defense on this position overlooking the Loire, common among the valley's oldest château sites.

Pray's ties to families connected to the royal court at Château d'Amboise situate this smaller château within the broader network of aristocratic residences that clustered around the more prominent royal seats of the Loire Valley.

As one of the very first Loire châteaux converted into a hotel, in 1955, Pray represents an early instance of a hospitality trend that would only become common decades later across the region's historic properties.

The château's immediate proximity to Château d'Amboise and Clos Lucé, Leonardo da Vinci's last home, gives guests staying at Pray direct access to two of the Loire Valley's most historically significant royal and Renaissance sites.

faqs.question: Are all the rooms at Château de Pray within the historic château?
faqs.answer: No — the 19 rooms are split between the main château and its outbuildings, within 5 hectares of gardens and parkland.

faqs.question: Since when has Château de Pray operated as a hotel?
faqs.answer: Since 1955, making it one of the very first Loire Valley châteaux to be converted into a hotel.

faqs.question: How close is Château de Pray to Château d'Amboise?
faqs.answer: About 5 minutes, along with Clos Lucé (Leonardo da Vinci's last home) — both within the same town of Amboise.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** In Amboise itself, Indre-et-Loire — 5 minutes from Château d'Amboise and Clos Lucé (Leonardo da Vinci's last home); about 30 minutes from Tours.

**Rooms & rates:** 19 rooms split between the historic château and its outbuildings, from €142/night.

**On-site:** 1-star Michelin restaurant, heated outdoor pool, 5 hectares of gardens and parkland, vegetable garden.

**Good to know:** One of the very first Loire château-hotels (open since 1955) — a long-established address, not a recent conversion. Some rooms sit in the outbuildings rather than the historic château itself.

**Combine with:** Château d'Amboise and Clos Lucé, both minutes away; Château de Chenonceau, about 30 minutes by car.
